title: Era 5 Quizzes (The Nineteenth Century) — Batch 5 of 7
subtitle: Questions 1–250 · Authenticated UGC NET Stems, Keys & Explanations

items.title: Quiz Q#1001 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Which work marked the first fictional publication under the pseudonym 'George Eliot', serialized in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1857 before appearing as a two-volume collection in 1858?
items.explanation: Scenes of Clerical Life (1857) was George Eliot's fictional debut, consisting of three novellas: 'The Sad Fortunes of the Reverend Amos Barton', 'Mr Gilfil's Love Story', and 'Janet's Repentance'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1002 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which novel by George Eliot does an upright, skilled carpenter of Hayslope suffer heartbreak over the vain dairymaid Hetty Sorrel before eventually marrying the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris?
items.explanation: Adam Bede is the titular hero of George Eliot's first full-length novel, Adam Bede (1859). The novel explores rural English morality, Hetty Sorrel's tragic child-murder, and Adam's mature union with Dinah Morris.

items.title: Quiz Q#1003 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which Victorian novel by George Eliot does the spirited and intellectually eager heroine Maggie Tulliver struggle between passionate impulse, familial duty to her brother Tom, and societal convention in St. Ogg's?
items.explanation: Maggie Tulliver is the central protagonist of George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss (1860). Her tragic life culminates in the dramatic flood of the River Floss, where she and Tom drown locked in a final embrace.

items.title: Quiz Q#1004 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Which semi-autobiographical novel by George Eliot, published in three volumes in April 1860 by William Blackwood, traces the turbulent lives of the Tulliver siblings at Dorlcote Mill?
items.explanation: The Mill on the Floss (1860) was published in three volumes after Eliot's success with Adam Bede. It draws heavily on Eliot's own childhood relationship with her brother Isaac Evans.

items.title: Quiz Q#1005 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which novel by George Eliot is a solitary linen weaver of Raveloe, embittered by a false accusation of theft in his youth, redeemed through the adoption of the golden-haired foundling child Eppie?
items.explanation: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861) tells the moral fable of Silas Marner, whose hoarded gold is stolen by Dunstan Cass and symbolically replaced by the orphaned child Eppie.

items.title: Quiz Q#1006 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Subtitled 'The Weaver of Raveloe', which 1861 novel by George Eliot presents a pastoral moral fable about the redemptive power of natural human affection over hoarded wealth?
items.explanation: Silas Marner (1861) is Eliot's concise masterpiece published by Blackwood. Eliot noted that it came to her as a sudden inspiration while planning her Italian historical novel Romola.

items.title: Quiz Q#1007 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which historical novel by George Eliot does the noble heroine Romola de' Bardi marry the opportunistic Greek scholar Tito Melema against the backdrop of 15th-century Renaissance Florence and Savonarola's religious rule?
items.explanation: Romola de' Bardi is the title character of George Eliot's Romola (1862–1863), set in Florence during the Italian Renaissance. Romola discovers moral purpose through the fiery preaching of Girolamo Savonarola.

items.title: Quiz Q#1008 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Which ambitious historical novel by George Eliot was serialized in The Cornhill Magazine between July 1862 and August 1863 after publisher George Smith paid a record £7,000 advance?
items.explanation: Romola (1862–1863) marked Eliot's departure from her usual publisher Blackwood to Cornhill Magazine. Illustrated by Frederic Leighton, it required immense historical research into Renaissance Florence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1009 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which masterpiece by George Eliot does the ardent and idealistic heroine Dorothea Brooke mistakenly marry the pedantic, elderly scholar Edward Casaubon in hopes of assisting his mythological research, the 'Key to all Mythologies'?
items.explanation: Dorothea Brooke is the heroine of Middlemarch (1871–1872). Her disillusionment with Casaubon and her subsequent bond with his cousin Will Ladislaw form one of the novel's central narrative strands.

items.title: Quiz Q#1010 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Study of Provincial Life', which monumental Victorian novel by George Eliot was originally published by Blackwood in eight bimonthly paperbound parts between December 1871 and December 1872?
items.explanation: Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life was issued in eight bi-monthly parts rather than standard monthly installments. Set during the 1832 Reform Act era, it weaves together the lives of Dorothea Brooke and Dr. Tertius Lydgate.

items.title: Quiz Q#1011 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: In which novel by George Eliot does the spirited, high-minded Gwendolen Harleth enter a disastrous marriage with the tyrannical aristocrat Henleigh Grandcourt to save her family from financial ruin?
items.explanation: Gwendolen Harleth is the proud, complex heroine of Daniel Deronda (1876). Her moral redemption is guided by the title character, Daniel Deronda, who simultaneously discovers his own Jewish heritage.

items.title: Quiz Q#1012 · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Eliot / Mary Ann Evans
items.stem: Published in eight monthly parts in 1876, which was George Eliot's final completed novel, uniquely contrasting the English country-house society of Gwendolen Harleth with the Jewish cultural identity of the title character?
items.explanation: Daniel Deronda (1876) was Eliot's final completed novel. It is celebrated for its dual plot and its groundbreaking proto-Zionist exploration of Jewish nationalism through Deronda, Mirah, and Mordecai.

items.title: Quiz Q#1013 · Herman Melville
items.stem: In which posthumously published novella by Herman Melville is a handsome, innocent young sailor condemned to hang after accidentally killing the malicious master-at-arms John Claggart with a single blow?
items.explanation: Billy Budd, Sailor (published 1924) dramatizes the fatal clash aboard HMS Bellipotent between the innocent foretopman Billy Budd and the envious master-at-arms John Claggart under Captain Edward Fairfax Vere.

items.title: Quiz Q#1014 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Which 19th-century American author wrote the naval novella in which the dying young sailor Billy Budd exclaims as his final words: "God bless Captain Vere!"?
items.explanation: This famous dying benediction appears in Herman Melville's Billy Budd, Sailor (1924), as Billy is hanged at the mainyard of Captain Vere's ship.

items.title: Quiz Q#1015 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Left in manuscript upon Herman Melville's death in 1891 and rediscovered by biographer Raymond Weaver before its first publication in 1924, which novella was Melville's final prose masterpiece?
items.explanation: Billy Budd, Sailor was written between 1888 and 1891 and left in manuscript. It was discovered among Melville's papers and published in 1924, sparking the major 20th-century Melville revival.

items.title: Quiz Q#1016 · Herman Melville
items.stem: In which 1846 travel narrative by Herman Melville does the sailor-narrator Tommo desert the whaling ship Dolly and live among the supposedly cannibalistic inhabitants of the Marquesas Islands?
items.explanation: Tommo is the narrator and fictionalized stand-in for Melville in Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life (1846), based on Melville's real-life four-week stay in the Typee Valley of Nuku Hiva.

items.title: Quiz Q#1017 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Which 1846 autobiographical South Seas romance was Herman Melville's debut literary work, published simultaneously in London by John Murray and New York by Wiley and Putnam?
items.explanation: Typee (1846) was Melville's sensational debut. In England it appeared in Murray's Colonial and Home Library under the title 'Narrative of a Four Months' Residence among the Natives of a Valley of the Marquesas Islands'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1018 · Herman Melville
items.stem: In Herman Melville's whaling epic Moby-Dick, which sole survivor of the Pequod famously introduces himself with the opening words: "Call me Ishmael"?
items.explanation: Ishmael is the narrator of Melville's Moby-Dick (1851), whose survival on Queequeg's carved coffin allows him to recount Captain Ahab's obsessive pursuit of the White Whale.

items.title: Quiz Q#1019 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Which 1851 masterpiece by Herman Melville was famously dedicated to Nathaniel Hawthorne "in token of my admiration for his genius"?
items.explanation: Melville dedicated Moby-Dick (1851) to his Pittsfield neighbor Nathaniel Hawthorne, whose dark romantic genius profoundly inspired Melville during the novel's revision.

items.title: Quiz Q#1020 · Herman Melville
items.stem: In which story by Herman Melville does a silent Wall Street legal copyist passively defy his employer's commands with the polite, repetitive refrain: "I would prefer not to"?
items.explanation: Bartleby is the enigmatic title character of Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street (1853), whose radical passive resistance culminates in his imprisonment and starvation in the Tombs.

items.title: Quiz Q#1021 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Who is the 19th-century author whose famous story features the enigmatic legal copyist whose polite yet unyielding answer to every request is: "I would prefer not to"?
items.explanation: This famous catchphrase is spoken repeatedly by the copyist Bartleby in Herman Melville's short story 'Bartleby, the Scrivener' (1853).

items.title: Quiz Q#1022 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Story of Wall-Street', which celebrated short fiction by Herman Melville was first serialized anonymously in Putnam's Monthly Magazine in 1853 before being collected in The Piazza Tales (1856)?
items.explanation: Bartleby, the Scrivener was published in two installments in Putnam's Monthly (November–December 1853). It is considered a pioneering forerunner of modernist absurdist literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1023 · Herman Melville
items.stem: In which 1855 novella by Herman Melville does the unsuspecting American captain Amasa Delano board the distressed slave ship San Dominick, entirely misreading the staged subservience of Babo?
items.explanation: Captain Amasa Delano is the gullible American captain in Benito Cereno (1855). Delano fails to realize that the enslaved Africans, led by Babo, have staged a revolt and forced Don Benito to act as a puppet captain.

items.title: Quiz Q#1024 · Herman Melville
items.stem: Based on a real incident recorded in Captain Amasa Delano's memoirs, which chilling tale of slave rebellion aboard the San Dominick was serialized in Putnam's Monthly Magazine in 1855?
items.explanation: Benito Cereno (1855) was collected in The Piazza Tales (1856). It is celebrated for its complex narrative perspective, gothic atmosphere, and critique of American racial blindness.

items.title: Quiz Q#1025 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which monumental five-volume work of art criticism did John Ruskin vigorously defend the landscape paintings of J. M. W. Turner and formulate his principles of 'truth to nature'?
items.explanation: Modern Painters (published in 5 volumes between 1843 and 1860) began as a defense of J. M. W. Turner, arguing that landscape art must be grounded in precise visual and scientific truth to nature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1026 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Which Victorian art critic and social theorist famously exhorted young artists to "go to Nature in all singleness of heart... having no other thoughts but how best to penetrate her meaning"?
items.explanation: This famous advice to young painters appears in Volume I of John Ruskin's Modern Painters (1843), providing the foundational philosophical inspiration for the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.

items.title: Quiz Q#1027 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Spanning five volumes published between 1843 and 1860, which major critical treatise by John Ruskin introduced the concepts of the 'Pathetic Fallacy' and 'the Penetrative Imagination'?
items.explanation: Modern Painters contains Ruskin's landmark coinages, including the 'Pathetic Fallacy' (Volume III, 1856), critiquing the sentimental projection of human emotions onto inanimate nature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1028 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which 1849 architectural treatise did John Ruskin codify the ethical and spiritual principles of building into seven moral 'lamps', including Sacrifice, Truth, Power, and Beauty?
items.explanation: The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849) formulated Ruskin's moral philosophy of architecture through seven principles: Sacrifice, Truth, Power, Beauty, Life, Memory, and Obedience.

items.title: Quiz Q#1029 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Who is the Victorian architectural critic who identified 'The Lamp of Sacrifice' as the fundamental principle demanding that man offer his precious labor and materials for the glory of God?
items.explanation: 'The Lamp of Sacrifice' is the opening chapter of John Ruskin's The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), arguing that ornamentation should embody dedicated, unselfish human devotion.

items.title: Quiz Q#1030 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Illustrated with fourteen etchings drawn by the author himself, which 1849 book by John Ruskin articulated his influential Gothic Revival philosophy of craftsmanship and civic memory?
items.explanation: The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849) was Ruskin's first work to feature his own detailed architectural illustrations, advocating Gothic architecture as an expression of spiritual integrity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1031 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which three-volume work (1851–1853) did John Ruskin trace the rise and decline of Venetian architecture to demonstrate that the moral, spiritual, and political health of a nation determines its artistic quality?
items.explanation: The Stones of Venice (1851–1853) examined Byzantine, Gothic, and Renaissance architecture in Venice, arguing that Renaissance classicism signaled moral and political corruption.

items.title: Quiz Q#1032 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Which Victorian social critic included the celebrated chapter 'The Nature of Gothic' in his architectural treatise The Stones of Venice, inspiring the Arts and Crafts movement of William Morris?
items.explanation: 'The Nature of Gothic' appears in Volume II of John Ruskin's The Stones of Venice (1853). William Morris famously printed it separately at the Kelmscott Press, calling it one of the most important texts of the century.

items.title: Quiz Q#1033 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Which influential three-volume work by John Ruskin, published between 1851 and 1853, famously celebrated the creative freedom and imperfect individuality of medieval Gothic stonecutters over mechanical division of labor?
items.explanation: The Stones of Venice (1851–1853) championed the medieval Gothic workman's liberty to express individual imperfection, contrasting it with the soul-crushing industrial factory systems of modern Britain.

items.title: Quiz Q#1034 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which radical 1860 critique of laissez-faire political economy did John Ruskin attack utilitarian economists and redefine wealth with the aphorism: 'There is no wealth but life'?
items.explanation: Unto This Last (1860) attacked John Stuart Mill, David Ricardo, and Adam Smith, arguing that true wealth consists in noble human life rather than mere monetary accumulation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1035 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Which Victorian critic and social reformer proclaimed in his treatise on political economy: "There is no wealth but life. Life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration"?
items.explanation: This celebrated dictum forms the core thesis of John Ruskin's Unto This Last (1860), which profoundly influenced Mahatma Gandhi's concept of Sarvodaya (welfare of all).

items.title: Quiz Q#1036 · John Ruskin
items.stem: First published in Thackeray's Cornhill Magazine in 1860 until reader outrage halted its serialization, which four-essay treatise by John Ruskin profoundly influenced Gandhi's philosophy of Sarvodaya?
items.explanation: Unto This Last was serialized in The Cornhill Magazine (August–November 1860). Thackeray stopped publication due to public outcry over Ruskin's socialist attack on capitalist economics.

items.title: Quiz Q#1037 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which popular 1865 lecture volume by John Ruskin are the two companion discourses titled 'Of Kings' Treasuries' (on reading and libraries) and 'Of Queens' Gardens' (on the noble domestic sphere of women)?
items.explanation: Sesame and Lilies (1865) collects two famous lectures delivered at Manchester in 1864: 'Of Kings' Treasuries' addressing literary culture and 'Of Queens' Gardens' outlining Victorian gender roles.

items.title: Quiz Q#1038 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Delivered as public lectures at Manchester in December 1864, which work by John Ruskin became his bestselling Victorian volume, containing his famous discussion of reading and female education?
items.explanation: Sesame and Lilies (1865) was Ruskin's most widely read book during the Victorian era, presenting education as a spiritual duty to cultivate social responsibility and noble literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1039 · John Ruskin
items.stem: In which 1866 collection of lectures addressed to working-class and military audiences did John Ruskin examine the three subjects of 'Work', 'Traffic', and 'War'?
items.explanation: The Crown of Wild Olive (1866) compiles three lectures on 'Work' (to working men), 'Traffic' (to the Bradford merchants), and 'War' (to the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich).

items.title: Quiz Q#1040 · John Ruskin
items.stem: Taking its title from the olive wreath awarded at the ancient Olympic Games, which 1866 volume by John Ruskin delivered sharp moral admonitions against competitive industrial greed and militarism?
items.explanation: The Crown of Wild Olive (1866) used the symbol of the ancient wild olive crown to urge that work, commerce, and national power be directed toward virtue rather than financial profit.

items.title: Quiz Q#1041 · Walt Whitman
items.stem: In which landmark 1855 collection of revolutionary free-verse poetry does the cosmic American persona proclaim: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself... I am large, I contain multitudes"?
items.explanation: Walt Whitman published the first edition of Leaves of Grass in 1855, containing twelve untitled poems including the masterpiece later titled 'Song of Myself'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1042 · Walt Whitman
items.stem: Printed at the author's own expense in Brooklyn in 1855 without his name on the title page, which revolutionary poetry volume was praised by Ralph Waldo Emerson as 'the most extraordinary piece of wit and wisdom that America has yet contributed'?
items.explanation: The first edition of Leaves of Grass (1855) was set in type partly by Whitman himself. Emerson sent him a famous congratulatory letter hailing its democratic innovation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1043 · Walt Whitman
items.stem: In which 1865 poetry collection did Walt Whitman reflect upon his personal experiences as a volunteer hospital nurse during the American Civil War, including the moving poem 'The Wound-Dresser'?
items.explanation: Drum-Taps (1865) chronicles Whitman's emotional journey during the American Civil War, moving from martial enthusiasm to haunting elegies for wounded and dying soldiers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1044 · Walt Whitman
items.stem: Which 1865 collection by Walt Whitman was supplemented with a sequel containing his celebrated elegies for the assassinated President Abraham Lincoln, 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' and 'O Captain! My Captain!'?
items.explanation: Following Lincoln's assassination in April 1865, Whitman added Sequel to Drum-Taps, containing 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' and 'O Captain! My Captain!'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1045 · Anna Sewell
items.stem: In which bestselling Victorian animal autobiography does a high-bred black horse narrate his experiences of kindness and cruelty under various human masters in Victorian England?
options: At the Back of the North Wind
items.explanation: Black Beauty: His Grooms and Companions, the Autobiography of a Horse (1877) was Anna Sewell's only novel, narrated from the first-person perspective of the horse.

items.title: Quiz Q#1046 · Anna Sewell
items.stem: Which Victorian author composed the classic first-person animal narrative that concludes peacefully with the narrator's reflection: "My troubles are all over, and I am at home"?
items.explanation: Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty (1877) from her sickbed, completing the novel shortly before her death in April 1878 to promote humane treatment of horses.

items.title: Quiz Q#1047 · Anna Sewell
items.stem: Subtitled 'The Autobiography of a Horse', which 1877 humanitarian novel by Anna Sewell successfully campaigned against the cruel Victorian use of the 'bearing rein'?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: Black Beauty (1877) became an international bestseller and a powerful instrument of animal welfare reform, contributing directly to the abolition of the painful bearing rein.

items.title: Quiz Q#1048 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: In which 1847 debut novel by Anne Brontë does the narrator, a gentle clergyman's daughter, confront the spoiled children and arrogant parents of the Bloomfield and Murray families as a governess?
items.explanation: Agnes Grey (1847) is Anne Brontë's realistic novel based on her own harrowing experiences as a governess, offering an unsparing look at the precarious social status of Victorian governesses.

items.title: Quiz Q#1049 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: Which Victorian novelist under the pen name 'Acton Bell' opened her debut novel about a governess with the assertion: "All true histories contain instruction; though, in some, the treasure may be hard to find"?
items.explanation: This moral declaration opens Agnes Grey (1847) by Anne Brontë (writing as Acton Bell), emphasizing the didactic and realistic purpose of her narrative.

items.title: Quiz Q#1050 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: Published together with Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights in a three-volume edition by Thomas Cautley Newby in December 1847, which realistic novel was Anne Brontë's fictional debut?
items.explanation: Newby issued Agnes Grey as the third volume of a three-decker set alongside the two volumes of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights in December 1847.

items.title: Quiz Q#1051 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: In which novel by Anne Brontë does the gentleman farmer Gilbert Markham fall in love with the reclusive artist Helen Graham, whose locked diary reveals her flight from her debauched husband Arthur Huntingdon?
items.explanation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) features Gilbert Markham's epistolary frame enclosing Helen Huntingdon's intimate diary, exposing the brutality and alcoholism of her husband Arthur.

items.title: Quiz Q#1052 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: Which 19th-century novelist defended her uncompromising depiction of alcoholism and marital abuse in a famous 1848 Preface, declaring: "I would rather whisper a few wholesome truths than much soft nonsense"?
items.explanation: Anne Brontë wrote this passionate defense in the Preface to the second edition of The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848), asserting the moral duty of a realist writer to depict vice truthfully.

items.title: Quiz Q#1053 · Anne Brontë
items.stem: Considered one of the earliest feminist novels in English literature, which 1848 work by Anne Brontë depicted a married woman defying English law by slamming her bedroom door against her husband and fleeing to protect her son?
items.explanation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) shocked contemporary critics with Helen Huntingdon's radical act of deserting her abusive husband to earn an independent living as an artist.

items.title: Quiz Q#1054 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: In which 1851 treatise did Victorian philosopher Herbert Spencer articulate his 'Law of Equal Freedom' and argue for extreme individualism and the minimal role of the state?
items.explanation: Social Statics: or, The Conditions essential to Human Happiness specified (1851) was Herbert Spencer's first major work, advocating radical laissez-faire libertarianism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1055 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: Published in London by John Chapman in 1851, which foundational work by Herbert Spencer anticipated his evolutionary social philosophy and established his concept of the 'Law of Equal Freedom'?
items.explanation: Social Statics (1851) introduced Spencer's ethical doctrine that every human being has freedom to do all that he wills, provided he infringes not the equal freedom of any other.

items.title: Quiz Q#1056 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: In which 1862 philosophical cornerstone of his 'Synthetic Philosophy' did Herbert Spencer define cosmic evolution as an integration of matter accompanied by a dissipation of motion?
items.explanation: First Principles (1862) laid down the general metaphysical and evolutionary foundations for Spencer's ambitious multi-volume System of Synthetic Philosophy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1057 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: Divided into two parts—'The Unknowable' (reconciling science and religion) and 'The Knowable' (the universal law of evolution)—which 1862 treatise inaugurated Herbert Spencer's Synthetic Philosophy?
items.explanation: First Principles (1862) famously posited the 'Unknowable' as the ultimate reality beyond both scientific investigation and religious dogma, followed by universal laws of evolution.

items.title: Quiz Q#1058 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: In which 1873 methodological textbook did Herbert Spencer analyze the various subjective biases—including the educational, patriotic, class, political, and theological biases—that hinder objective social science?
items.explanation: The Study of Sociology (1873) was commissioned by Edward Youmans for the International Scientific Series, establishing methodological guidelines for systematic sociology.

items.title: Quiz Q#1059 · Herbert Spencer
items.stem: Which 1873 work by Herbert Spencer was instrumental in establishing sociology as an academic discipline in Britain and the United States, arguing for the objective scientific analysis of social phenomena?
items.explanation: The Study of Sociology (1873) was widely adopted as a university textbook, popularizing evolutionary sociology and demonstrating how personal biases distort social investigation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1060 · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.stem: In which infamous 1868 Saturday Review essay (collected in 1883) did anti-feminist writer Elizabeth Lynn Linton fiercely condemn modern young women who aped Parisian fashion and rejected traditional domestic modesty?
options: The True History of Joshua Davidson
The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays
items.explanation: Eliza Lynn Linton published 'The Girl of the Period' in the Saturday Review on 14 March 1868, creating a Victorian sensation with her savage critique of modern independent womanhood.

items.title: Quiz Q#1061 · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.stem: Which Victorian journalist and novelist caused a public scandal with her 1868 attack on the modern young woman, warning that: "Men are afraid of her; and having every reason to be afraid of her, they put her down as a fast girl"?
items.explanation: Elizabeth Lynn Linton coined the catchphrase 'The Girl of the Period' in her biting essay of that title, portraying the modern English girl as vain, loud, and unsuited for marriage.

items.title: Quiz Q#1062 · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.stem: First published anonymously in the Saturday Review in March 1868 before appearing as the title piece of an 1883 two-volume collection, which essay by Elizabeth Lynn Linton coined one of the most famous cultural catchphrases of Victorian journalism?
options: The Girl of the Period and Other Social Essays
items.explanation: 'The Girl of the Period' became a widespread cultural reference point in Victorian journalism, debate, and cartoons, epitomizing conservative anxiety over emerging female independence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1063 · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.stem: In which 1885 novel by Elizabeth Lynn Linton does the author use a male protagonist's narrative mask to write a thinly disguised, candid autobiographical account of her own intellectual struggles and failed marriage?
options: The True History of Joshua Davidson
items.explanation: The Autobiography of Christopher Kirkland (1885) is an autobiographical roman-à-clef in which Linton transposes her own life, career, and marriage to radical editor W. J. Linton onto a male hero.

items.title: Quiz Q#1064 · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Elizabeth Lynn Linton
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Richard Bentley in 1885, which novel by Elizabeth Lynn Linton is renowned among literary historians as a gender-reversed autobiography reflecting the author's unconventional life?
items.explanation: In The Autobiography of Christopher Kirkland, Linton inverted her gender to speak freely about her love affairs, agnosticism, and intellectual development in Victorian London.

items.title: Quiz Q#1065 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which pastoral elegy by Matthew Arnold does an Oxford student abandon academic pedantry to join a band of wanderers, searching for a secret, intuitive wisdom away from 'the strange disease of modern life'?
items.explanation: The Scholar-Gipsy (1853) is based on a story in Joseph Glanvill's The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), contrasting the gipsy's single-minded spiritual quest with modern Victorian skepticism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1066 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which Victorian poet-critic urged the wandering Oxford scholar to maintain his solitary quest, writing: "Thou waitest for the spark from heaven! and we, / Light half-believers of our casual creeds..."?
items.explanation: These famous lines appear in Matthew Arnold's 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853), lamenting Victorian intellectual indecision, doubt, and sick fatigue.

items.title: Quiz Q#1067 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Drawing its narrative inspiration from Joseph Glanvill's 1661 book The Vanity of Dogmatizing and celebrating the Cumner hills near Oxford, which 1853 poem is one of Matthew Arnold's finest pastoral achievements?
items.explanation: 'The Scholar-Gipsy' was written in 1853 and published in Poems (1853). It concludes with the famous extended epic simile of the Tyrian trader fleeing the intrusive Greek coasters.

items.title: Quiz Q#1068 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which 1849 title poem by Matthew Arnold does a wandering youth drink from Circe's enchanted golden cup in the presence of Ulysses, experiencing visionary poetic ecstasies without divine suffering?
items.explanation: 'The Strayed Reveller' is the title poem of Arnold's 1849 volume, dramatizing the poetic consciousness suspended between the intoxicating vision of Circe and the heroic labor of Ulysses.

items.title: Quiz Q#1069 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Published anonymously in 1849 under the single initial 'A.', which was Matthew Arnold's debut poetry collection, containing 'The Forsaken Merman' and 'Resignation'?
options: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems
Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems
items.explanation: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems (1849) was published by B. Fellows under the pseudonym 'A.' Arnold withdrew the collection shortly after publication after selling only a few copies.

items.title: Quiz Q#1070 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which dramatic poem by Matthew Arnold does an ancient Greek philosopher, disillusioned with intellectual isolation and the loss of joy in modern thought, leap to his death into the crater of Mount Etna?
items.explanation: Empedocles on Etna (1852) dramatizes the psychological crisis of the pre-Socratic philosopher Empedocles, whose song of cosmic detachment precedes his suicidal leap into the volcano.

items.title: Quiz Q#1071 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which Victorian poet composed the philosophical lyric wherein the troubled Greek sage Empedocles chants to his harp: "Is it so small a thing / To have enjoy'd the sun, / To have lived light in the spring..."?
items.explanation: This stoic hymn to earthly contentment is sung by Empedocles in Act I, Scene 2 of Matthew Arnold's Empedocles on Etna (1852).

items.title: Quiz Q#1072 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which major dramatic poem did Matthew Arnold notoriously exclude from his 1853 Poems on the grounds that it depicted a situation in which 'everything is to be endured, nothing to be done'?
items.explanation: Arnold suppressed Empedocles on Etna in 1853, famously arguing in his Preface that passive mental distress devoid of action does not produce genuine poetic pleasure. He restored it in 1867 at Robert Browning's request.

items.title: Quiz Q#1073 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which 1853 narrative poem by Matthew Arnold, drawn from the Persian national epic Shahnameh, does the young Tartar warrior Sohrab fight an unwitting mortal duel with his own father on the sands of the Oxus?
items.explanation: 'Sohrab and Rustum: An Episode' is Matthew Arnold's celebrated Homeric narrative poem, published in Poems (1853), culminating in Rustum's grief upon identifying his dying son's seal.

items.title: Quiz Q#1074 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which Victorian critic and poet argued in a famous 1853 Preface that poetry must not depict states of mind where "a continuous state of mental distress is prolonged... in which there is everything to be endured, nothing to be done"?
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold's Preface to Poems (1853) is a foundational document of Victorian neoclassical poetics, urging modern poets to return to the grand actions of ancient classical models.

items.title: Quiz Q#1075 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Published in 1853 with a landmark critical Preface repudiating Romantic subjectivism, which collection was the first volume to appear under Matthew Arnold's full name?
items.explanation: Poems (1853) was Arnold's first volume published under his own name by Longmans. It featured the 1853 Preface, 'Sohrab and Rustum', and 'The Scholar-Gipsy'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1076 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which landmark 1865 critical volume did Matthew Arnold define criticism as "a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world"?
items.explanation: Essays in Criticism (First Series, 1865) collected Arnold's lectures delivered as Professor of Poetry at Oxford, opening with 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1077 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Containing seminal essays on Heinrich Heine, Maurice de Guérin, and Marcus Aurelius, which 1865 collection established Matthew Arnold as the preeminent English literary critic of the Victorian age?
items.explanation: Essays in Criticism (1865) championed European cosmopolitanism, intellectual disinterestedness, and spiritual flexibility against narrow English provincialism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1078 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which 1867 poetry collection did Matthew Arnold restore Empedocles on Etna to print at the personal urging of Robert Browning, alongside the pastoral elegy 'Thyrsis'?
items.explanation: New Poems (1867) was Arnold's last major original poetry collection, featuring 'Thyrsis' (commemorating Arthur Hugh Clough), 'Dover Beach', and the restored Empedocles on Etna.

items.title: Quiz Q#1079 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which Victorian poet commemorated his close friend Arthur Hugh Clough in the pastoral elegy 'Thyrsis', writing: "Too quick despairer, wherefore wilt thou go? / Soon will the high Midsummer pomps come on"?
items.explanation: These lines open stanza 7 of Matthew Arnold's 'Thyrsis' (1867), his great companion pastoral elegy to 'The Scholar-Gipsy', mourning Clough's premature death in Florence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1080 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which 1867 volume by Matthew Arnold marked his final important gathering of verse, containing 'Dover Beach', 'Thyrsis', 'Rugby Chapel', and 'Obermann Once More'?
items.explanation: New Poems (1867) effectively concluded Arnold's primary career as a poet, as he subsequently turned almost entirely to prose cultural, social, and religious criticism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1081 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which celebrated 1867 lyric does Matthew Arnold look across the English Channel toward the French coast, hearing the 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar' of the Sea of Faith?
items.explanation: 'Dover Beach' is Arnold's most famous lyric, dramatizing the retreat of religious certainty and concluding with the stark plea for interpersonal love on a 'darkling plain'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1082 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Who is the Victorian poet whose iconic poem 'Dover Beach' contains the poignant lovers' plea: "Ah, love, let us be true / To one another! for the world, which seems / To lie before us like a land of dreams..."?
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold composed these famous closing lines of 'Dover Beach' (published 1867), contrasting the illusion of the modern world with its lack of peace, joy, and light.

items.title: Quiz Q#1083 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: First drafted in 1851 during the author's honeymoon and published in New Poems (1867), which poem concludes with the haunting image of 'ignorant armies' clashing by night on a darkling plain?
items.explanation: 'Dover Beach' (1867) ends with the enduring metaphor of modern human alienation: 'And we are here as on a darkling plain / Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight, / Where ignorant armies clash by night.'

items.title: Quiz Q#1084 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In which 1869 masterpiece of social criticism did Matthew Arnold categorize English society into 'Barbarians' (the aristocracy), 'Philistines' (the middle class), and 'Populace' (the working class)?
items.explanation: Culture and Anarchy (1869) analyzed the social divisions of Victorian Britain, arguing that 'Culture'—defined as sweetness and light—is the only remedy against spiritual anarchy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1085 · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which 1869 treatise by Matthew Arnold formulated the famous dialectic between 'Hebraism' (strictness of conscience and moral duty) and 'Hellenism' (spontaneity of consciousness and intellectual clarity)?
items.explanation: In Chapter 4 of Culture and Anarchy ('Hebraism and Hellenism'), Arnold argued that English Puritan culture was over-Hebraized and needed Hellenic sweetness and light to attain balanced human perfection.

items.title: Quiz Q#1086 · George MacDonald
items.stem: In which 1858 fantasy novel by George MacDonald does the young protagonist Anodos enter the mysterious realm of Fairy Land on his twenty-first birthday, confronting spiritual perils and his own dark Shadow?
options: At the Back of the North Wind
items.explanation: Anodos (whose Greek name means 'pathless' or 'wayfarer') is the protagonist of Phantastes: A Faerie Romance for Men and Women (1858), a pioneering classic of adult fantasy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1087 · George MacDonald
items.stem: Which Scottish author and Christian mythopoeic pioneer composed the 1858 adult fantasy romance Phantastes, which C. S. Lewis credited with 'baptizing' his imagination?
items.explanation: George MacDonald's Phantastes (1858) profoundly influenced modern fantasy literature. C. S. Lewis famously acknowledged MacDonald as his primary literary and spiritual master.

items.title: Quiz Q#1088 · George MacDonald
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Faerie Romance for Men and Women', which 1858 book by George MacDonald was the first prose fantasy novel written in the English language?
options: The Well at the World's End
items.explanation: Phantastes (1858) inaugurated modern English fantasy. MacDonald drew upon German Romantic Novalis and E. T. A. Hoffmann to create a visionary allegorical journey of spiritual maturation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1089 · George MacDonald
items.stem: In which 1872 children's fantasy novel by George MacDonald does eight-year-old Princess Irene discover her magical great-great-grandmother spinning an invisible protective thread in the palace attic?
options: At the Back of the North Wind
items.explanation: The Princess and the Goblin (1872) features Princess Irene and the miner's boy Curdie, who defend the mountain kingdom against underground goblins who have soft, vulnerable feet.

items.title: Quiz Q#1090 · George MacDonald
items.stem: Published in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes, which children's classic by George MacDonald depicts the miner boy Curdie and Princess Irene outwitting subterranean goblins?
options: At the Back of the North Wind
items.explanation: The Princess and the Goblin was published by Strahan & Co. in 1872 after serializing in Good Words for the Young. Hughes's illustrations became iconic in Victorian children's literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1091 · George MacDonald
items.stem: In which dark, metaphysical 1895 fantasy novel by George MacDonald does Mr. Vane follow a mysterious raven through an attic mirror into a multi-dimensional universe where he encounters Adam, Eve, and the vampire-queen Lilith?
options: At the Back of the North Wind
items.explanation: Lilith (1895) is MacDonald's final, complex masterpiece of theological fantasy, exploring universal salvation, death as spiritual sleep, and redemption through suffering.

items.title: Quiz Q#1092 · George MacDonald
items.stem: Who is the Scottish author of the 1895 visionary novel Lilith, in which the mysterious raven-librarian Mr. Raven turns out to be the biblical progenitor Adam?
items.explanation: George MacDonald published Lilith in 1895. The novel offers a profound Christian allegory of the soul's surrender of the self, culminating in the redemption of Adam's rebellious first wife, Lilith.

items.title: Quiz Q#1093 · George MacDonald
items.stem: Which 1895 dark allegorical fantasy by George MacDonald is widely regarded by modern scholars as one of the most intense theological romances in Victorian literature, exploring the defeat of cosmic evil?
items.explanation: Lilith (1895) challenged traditional Victorian orthodoxy with its vision of universalist Christian restoration (apokatastasis), wherein even the demonic Lilith eventually yields to divine love.

items.title: Quiz Q#1094 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: In which 1874 social novel by Lal Behari Day is the hard, unvarnished life of a Bengali peasant cultivator (raiyat) realistically depicted from birth and village schooling to debt and death?
items.explanation: Govinda Samanta; or, the History of a Bengal Raiyat (1874) won a prize offered by Baboo Joy Kissen Mookerjee for the best fictional work illustrating rural Bengali peasant life.

items.title: Quiz Q#1095 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: Which 19th-century Indian author and educator wrote the pioneering realistic novel Govinda Samanta, quoting Thomas Gray's line about "the short and simple annals of the poor" in his preface?
items.explanation: Reverend Lal Behari Day (1824–1894) was a Christian missionary and scholar whose Govinda Samanta presented the first realistic sociological depiction of the Bengali peasantry in English.

items.title: Quiz Q#1096 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: Published in two volumes by Macmillan in London in 1874 (and later reissued as Bengal Peasant Life), which landmark novel by Lal Behari Day won high acclaim from Charles Darwin for its social fidelity?
items.explanation: Govinda Samanta was reissued by Macmillan in 1878 as Bengal Peasant Life. Charles Darwin read and praised the book for its vivid, truthful documentation of rural agricultural society.

items.title: Quiz Q#1097 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: Which 1883 collection by Lal Behari Day preserves traditional oral stories—such as 'The Story of the Prince Sobur' and 'The Field of Bones'—as recounted by rural Bengali grandmothers and village storytellers?
items.explanation: Folk-Tales of Bengal (1883) was compiled by Lal Behari Day directly from vernacular oral storytellers, making Bengali folklore accessible to international English-speaking audiences.

items.title: Quiz Q#1098 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: Which 19th-century scholar published Folk-Tales of Bengal with Macmillan in 1883, transcribing traditional Bengali fairy tales that conclude with the formulaic rhyming refrain: "Thus my story endeth, / The Natiya-thorn withereth..."?
items.explanation: Lal Behari Day preserved traditional Bengali storytelling formulas in Folk-Tales of Bengal, including the classic closing couplet translated from vernacular village tale-tellers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1099 · Lal Behari Day
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lal Behari Day
items.stem: Undertaken at the suggestion of Richard Temple (Governor of Bengal), which 1883 volume by Lal Behari Day was a foundational contribution to modern Indian folklore studies in English?
items.explanation: Folk-Tales of Bengal (1883) was celebrated by folklorists worldwide. Day took care to record the tales without European literary alterations, preserving genuine indigenous folk traditions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1100 · Michael Madhusudan Dutt
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Michael Madhusudan Dutt
items.stem: In which 1849 narrative poem in English by Michael Madhusudan Dutt is the Rajput hero Prithviraj Chauhan celebrated for abducting Princess Sanyogita from the swayamvara at Kannauj?
items.explanation: The Captive Ladie (1849) is Michael Madhusudan Dutt's narrative poem in octosyllabic verse based on the historical romance of Prithviraj Chauhan and the princess of Kannauj.

items.title: Quiz Q#1101 · Michael Madhusudan Dutt
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Michael Madhusudan Dutt
items.stem: Printed at the Advertiser Press in Madras in 1849 under the pseudonym 'Timothy Penpoetry', which English verse tale was Michael Madhusudan Dutt's most significant English-language poetic work?
items.explanation: The Captive Ladie was published in Madras in 1849. Its mixed critical reception convinced Dutt to abandon English verse and dedicate his revolutionary poetic genius to his native Bengali.

items.title: Quiz Q#1102 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: In which sensation novel by Wilkie Collins does the young drawing master Walter Hartright encounter the mysterious Anne Catherick on the moonlit road from Hampstead to London?
items.explanation: Walter Hartright is the hero and chief narrator of The Woman in White (1860). His nocturnal meeting with Anne Catherick draws him into the sinister plot concocted by Sir Percival Glyde and Count Fosco.

items.title: Quiz Q#1103 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: Serialized in Charles Dickens's journal All the Year Round from November 1859 to August 1860, which bestselling work by Wilkie Collins established the Victorian 'sensation novel' genre?
items.explanation: The Woman in White was a publishing phenomenon in All the Year Round, featuring multiple epistolary testimonies, marital fraud, asylum imprisonment, and the flamboyant villain Count Fosco.

items.title: Quiz Q#1104 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: In which 1862 novel by Wilkie Collins does the disinherited, fiercely determined Magdalen Vanstone use theatrical disguise and a sham marriage to recover the family fortune stolen by her scheming relatives?
items.explanation: Magdalen Vanstone is the daring heroine of No Name (1862). After learning that their parents were unmarried at their birth, Magdalen rebels against Victorian illegitimacy laws.

items.title: Quiz Q#1105 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: Serialized in All the Year Round between March 1862 and January 1863, which Wilkie Collins sensation novel critiques the harsh Victorian legal doctrine of bastardy through the rebellious Magdalen Vanstone?
items.explanation: No Name (1862) challenged English inheritance laws that stripped illegitimate children of all legal identity and fortune upon their parents' sudden death.

items.title: Quiz Q#1106 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: In which complex 1866 sensation novel by Wilkie Collins are two cousins of the same name—one privileged, one illegitimate and tormented—hunted by the beautiful and deadly poisoner Lydia Gwilt?
items.explanation: Armadale (1866) interweaves the destinies of Allan Armadale and Ozias Midwinter (also born Allan Armadale). Lydia Gwilt is one of the most compelling female villains in Victorian fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1107 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: Serialized in The Cornhill Magazine from November 1864 to June 1866 with striking illustrations by George Thomas, which dark sensation novel was one of Wilkie Collins's most elaborate plotted works?
items.explanation: Armadale was published in two volumes by Smith, Elder in 1866, exploring fatalism, hereditary murder, psychological dreams, and the mercenary crimes of Lydia Gwilt.

items.title: Quiz Q#1108 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: In which 1868 masterpiece by Wilkie Collins is a priceless Indian gem stolen from the Yorkshire country house of Rachel Verinder, solved by Sergeant Cuff through forensic detection?
items.explanation: The Moonstone (1868) is widely hailed as the first and greatest modern English detective novel, featuring Sergeant Cuff, the house steward Gabriel Betteredge, and multiple eyewitness narratives.

items.title: Quiz Q#1109 · Wilkie Collins
items.stem: Celebrated by T. S. Eliot as 'the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels', which 1868 work by Wilkie Collins pioneered classic tropes of detective fiction including the country-house theft and red herrings?
items.explanation: The Moonstone (1868) was serialized in All the Year Round. Eliot's famous praise highlighted Collins's sophisticated multiple-narrator technique and the groundbreaking character of Sergeant Cuff.

items.title: Quiz Q#1110 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: In which 1854 abolitionist poetry collection does Frances Ellen Watkins Harper dramatize the anguish of a bondwoman having her child torn from her arms in the harrowing poem 'The Slave Mother'?
options: Moses: A Story of the Nile
items.explanation: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects (1854) was Frances E. W. Harper's major breakthrough poetry collection, selling over 10,000 copies and aiding the American abolitionist movement.

items.title: Quiz Q#1111 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: Which 19th-century African-American poet and orator opened her famous abolitionist poem 'The Slave Mother' with the dramatic cry: "Heard you that shriek? It rose / So wildly on the air..."?
items.explanation: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper included 'The Slave Mother' in Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects (1854), evoking deep emotional outrage against the brutality of slave auctions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1112 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: Published in Boston in 1854 with a supportive preface by prominent abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, which collection established Frances Ellen Watkins Harper as an influential poetic voice?
items.explanation: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects (1854) was widely distributed across anti-slavery fairs, combining anti-slavery protests with temperance and Christian humanitarian themes.

items.title: Quiz Q#1113 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: In which 1892 Reconstruction-era novel by Frances E. W. Harper does the mixed-race heroine, sold into slavery despite her white upbringing, refuse to 'pass' for white and dedicate her life to educating the freed community?
items.explanation: Iola Leroy, or Shadows Uplifted (1892) is Frances E. W. Harper's landmark novel exploring race, post-Civil War reconstruction, African-American family reunification, and racial uplift.

items.title: Quiz Q#1114 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: Which pioneering 19th-century African-American author created the courageous heroine Iola Leroy, who proudly affirms her black identity with the words: "I am not ashamed of it... I belong to that race"?
items.explanation: Frances E. W. Harper was sixty-seven when she published Iola Leroy (1892), one of the first published novels by an African-American woman.

items.title: Quiz Q#1115 · Frances E. W. Harper
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Frances E. W. Harper
items.stem: Subtitled 'Shadows Uplifted', which 1892 novel by Frances E. W. Harper is a cornerstone of early African-American feminist literature, depicting black empowerment and social reconstruction after the Civil War?
items.explanation: Iola Leroy, or Shadows Uplifted (1892) challenged plantation romance myths, celebrating African-American dignity, literacy, and community rebuilding.

items.title: Quiz Q#1116 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: In which 1856 adventure novel by R. M. Ballantyne, drawn from the author's six years of service with the Hudson's Bay Company, does young Charley Kennedy embark on fur-trading expeditions in the Canadian wilderness?
items.explanation: The Young Fur Traders (1856) was Ballantyne's debut novel for boys, originally titled Snowflakes and Sunbeams, drawing on his authentic experiences in the Canadian fur trade.

items.title: Quiz Q#1117 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: Which Scottish boys' adventure novelist drew upon his personal employment in Canada with the Hudson's Bay Company to write The Young Fur Traders (1856)?
items.explanation: Robert Michael Ballantyne (1825–1894) spent six years in the Canadian wild as a fur trader before returning to Edinburgh to become a prolific adventure writer.

items.title: Quiz Q#1118 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: First published in Edinburgh in 1856 under the initial title Snowflakes and Sunbeams, which adventure tale established R. M. Ballantyne's reputation as a master storyteller of Canadian frontier life?
items.explanation: Snowflakes and Sunbeams; or, The Young Fur Traders (1856) was published by Thomas Nelson, inaugurating Ballantyne's long series of juvenile adventure books.

items.title: Quiz Q#1119 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: In which 1858 South Seas Robinsonade by R. M. Ballantyne are three British youths—Ralph Rover, Jack Martin, and Peterkin Gay—shipwrecked on an uninhabited Polynesian island, where they encounter hostile pirates and cannibals?
items.explanation: The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean (1858) is Ballantyne's most famous novel, celebrating British pluck, Christian missions, and juvenile survival.

items.title: Quiz Q#1120 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: Which Victorian author opened his celebrated castaway novel The Coral Island with an authorial address declaring: "I present my book specially to boys, in the earnest hope that they may derive valuable information as well as amusement..."?
items.explanation: R. M. Ballantyne addressed The Coral Island (1858) specifically to young boys, pairing thrilling adventure with didactic evangelical Christianity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1121 · R. M. Ballantyne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · R. M. Ballantyne
items.stem: Which classic 1858 Victorian castaway tale by R. M. Ballantyne directly provided the thematic target and ironic character prototypes for William Golding's 1954 dystopian novel Lord of the Flies?
items.explanation: William Golding wrote Lord of the Flies (1954) as a dark, realistic inversion of Ballantyne's optimistic imperialist classic The Coral Island (1858), reusing the names Ralph, Jack, and Peterkin.

items.title: Quiz Q#1122 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: In which groundbreaking 1863 scientific treatise did Thomas Henry Huxley examine comparative primate anatomy and fossil Neanderthal remains to prove humanity's evolutionary kinship with anthropoid apes?
options: Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature
items.explanation: Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature (1863) was the first comprehensive book dedicated to human evolution, published eight years before Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man (1871).

items.title: Quiz Q#1123 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: Which Victorian biologist, famous as 'Darwin's Bulldog', demonstrated in his 1863 treatise on human evolution that "the structural differences which separate Man from the Gorilla and the Chimpanzee are not so great as those which separate the Gorilla from the lower apes"?
items.explanation: Thomas Henry Huxley marshaled precise anatomical evidence in Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature (1863) to defend the evolutionary continuity between apes and humans.

items.title: Quiz Q#1124 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: Published in London in 1863 by Williams and Norgate, which book by Thomas Henry Huxley famously resolved the 'Great Hippocampus Question' debate against conservative anatomist Richard Owen?
options: Evidence as to Man’s Place in Nature
items.explanation: Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature demolished Richard Owen's claim that the human brain possesses unique anatomical structures (like the hippocampus minor) absent in apes.

items.title: Quiz Q#1125 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: In which 1870 volume of popular lectures and essays did Thomas Henry Huxley collect 'A Piece of Chalk' and 'On the Physical Basis of Life', expounding the materialist protoplasm theory?
options: Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature
items.explanation: Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews (1870) collected Huxley's famous public lectures, including 'On a Piece of Chalk' (1868) and 'On the Physical Basis of Life' (1868).

items.title: Quiz Q#1126 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: Which Victorian scientist and agnostic thinker described Francis Bacon's inductive method as the precursor to biological science, calling Darwin's Origin of Species "the Novum Organon of biology" in his Lay Sermons?
items.explanation: Thomas Henry Huxley celebrated Darwin's revolutionary achievement in Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews (1870), establishing evolutionary theory as the guiding foundation of modern biology.

items.title: Quiz Q#1127 · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Thomas Henry Huxley
items.stem: Published by Macmillan in 1870, which essay collection by Thomas Henry Huxley championed liberal scientific education and the intellectual emancipation of working-class citizens?
options: Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature
items.explanation: Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews (1870) was Huxley's widely influential volume making advanced scientific concepts accessible to general Victorian readers and promoting secular science education.

items.title: Quiz Q#1128 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: In which celebrated Pre-Raphaelite poem by Dante Gabriel Rossetti does a deceased maiden lean out from the golden bar of Heaven, weeping as she longs for her earthly lover to join her?
items.explanation: The Blessed Damozel (drafted 1847, published 1850) is Dante Gabriel Rossetti's most famous lyric, written as a conscious reversal of Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Raven'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1129 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Which Pre-Raphaelite poet-painter opened his iconic lyric of heavenly longing with the lines: "The blessed damozel leaned out / From the gold bar of Heaven; / Her eyes were deeper than the depth / Of waters stilled at even"?
items.explanation: Dante Gabriel Rossetti composed 'The Blessed Damozel' at age nineteen, illustrating it with his own famous dual-panel painting depicting the damozel looking down at her earthbound lover.

items.title: Quiz Q#1130 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: First printed in the opening February 1850 issue of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood's short-lived periodical The Germ, which poem was Dante Gabriel Rossetti's earliest literary masterpiece?
items.explanation: 'The Blessed Damozel' appeared in The Germ (1850). Rossetti subsequently revised the poem extensively for his 1870 Poems and 1881 Ballads and Sonnets.

items.title: Quiz Q#1131 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: In which landmark sonnet sequence by Dante Gabriel Rossetti does the speaker meditate across 102 sonnets on youthful passion, artistic creation, physical intimacy, and the grief of lost love?
items.explanation: The House of Life is Rossetti's monumental sonnet sequence, published in part in Poems (1870) and completed in Ballads and Sonnets (1881), divided into 'Youth and Change' and 'Change and Fate'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1132 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Which Victorian poet defined the poetic miniature in the introductory sonnet to The House of Life with the famous line: "A Sonnet is a moment's monument, / Memorial from the Soul's eternity / To one dead deathless hour"?
items.explanation: Dante Gabriel Rossetti composed this iconic introductory sonnet for the complete 1881 edition of The House of Life, encapsulating the aesthetic dedication to capturing intense sensory moments.

items.title: Quiz Q#1133 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Attacked by Robert Buchanan in his 1871 contemporary pamphlet 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' for its sensual frankness in sonnets like 'Nuptial Sleep', which sonnet sequence was Dante Gabriel Rossetti's crowning achievement?
items.explanation: The House of Life provoked Robert Buchanan's venomous attack in The Contemporary Review ('The Fleshly School of Poetry'), which plunged Rossetti into deep psychological depression and paranoia.

items.title: Quiz Q#1134 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: In which 1861 scholarly and poetic translation volume did Dante Gabriel Rossetti introduce Victorian readers to the Dolce Stil Novo, translating Dante Alighieri's Vita Nuova and poets from Guido Cavalcanti to Cino da Pistoia?
items.explanation: The Early Italian Poets (1861, reissued in 1874 as Dante and His Circle) established Rossetti as an exquisite translator of medieval Tuscan love poetry and Dante's Vita Nuova.

items.title: Quiz Q#1135 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Financed in part by John Ruskin and published by Smith, Elder in 1861, which landmark translation volume by Dante Gabriel Rossetti made medieval Italian lyric poetry accessible in English?
items.explanation: The Early Italian Poets (1861) was subsidized by Ruskin, who guaranteed the publisher against financial loss because of his deep admiration for Rossetti's fidelity to Dante.

items.title: Quiz Q#1136 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: In which dramatic ballad from Dante Gabriel Rossetti's 1870 Poems does a scorned woman melt a wax effigy of her unfaithful lover Keith of Ewern over a fire for three days, destroying his soul?
items.explanation: 'Sister Helen' is Rossetti's chilling literary ballad featuring an incremental chorus between Sister Helen and her little brother as she practices lethal sympathetic witchcraft.

items.title: Quiz Q#1137 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Which Pre-Raphaelite poet-painter wrote the grief-stricken nature lyric 'The Woodspurge', ending with the stark observation: "One thing then learnt remained to me, / The woodspurge has a cup of three"?
items.explanation: 'The Woodspurge' (written 1856, published in Poems 1870) records the acute perceptual fixation that accompanies overwhelming psychological sorrow.

items.title: Quiz Q#1138 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Which 1870 volume by Dante Gabriel Rossetti had its manuscripts famously exhumed from the Highgate Cemetery grave of his wife Elizabeth Siddal before its publication by F. S. Ellis?
items.explanation: In October 1869, Rossetti obtained official permission to exhume the poetry manuscript he had buried in Elizabeth Siddal's coffin in 1862, publishing it as Poems in 1870.

items.title: Quiz Q#1139 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: In which 1881 historical ballad from Ballads and Sonnets does Catherine Douglas narrate how she barred the royal chamber door with her bare arm to protect King James I of Scotland from assassination?
items.explanation: 'The King's Tragedy' is Rossetti's epic ballad of Catherine Douglas ('Kate Barlass'), who earned her nickname by thrusting her arm into the door-staple against the King's assassins.

items.title: Quiz Q#1140 · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Dante Gabriel Rossetti
items.stem: Published in 1881 shortly before the author's death, which volume completed Dante Gabriel Rossetti's sonnet sequence The House of Life and included major narrative ballads like 'Rose Mary' and 'The King's Tragedy'?
items.explanation: Ballads and Sonnets (1881) was Rossetti's final collection, containing the complete 102-sonnet House of Life and his major narrative verse tales.

items.title: Quiz Q#1141 · George Meredith
items.stem: In which 1859 novel by George Meredith does Sir Austin Feverel subject his son to an elaborate, sheltered educational 'System' designed to keep him free from female corruptions, leading to tragic disaster?
items.explanation: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel (1859) dramatizes Sir Austin's rigid educational system, which blinds him to natural human passion and causes Richard's disastrous secret marriage to Lucy Desborough.

items.title: Quiz Q#1142 · George Meredith
items.stem: Subtitled 'A History of a Father and Son', which 1859 novel by George Meredith was banned by Mudie's Circulating Library for supposed moral impropriety?
items.explanation: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel (1859) was condemned by Mudie's Library for its candid treatment of sexuality, but is now recognized as a groundbreaking psychological novel.

items.title: Quiz Q#1143 · George Meredith
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in 1859—the same watershed year that saw Adam Bede and Origin of Species—which novel was George Meredith's first major fictional triumph?
items.explanation: The Ordeal of Richard Feverel appeared in 1859. Meredith's poetic style, psychological realism, and ironic commentary marked a new departure in Victorian fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1144 · George Meredith
items.stem: In which 1879 comic masterpiece by George Meredith does Sir Willoughby Patterne, an insufferably self-absorbed baronet, drive away his spirited fiancée Clara Middleton through his suffocating vanity?
items.explanation: Sir Willoughby Patterne is the title character of The Egoist (1879). Clara Middleton gradually recognizes his tyrannical self-worship and escapes with the scholar Vernon Whitford.

items.title: Quiz Q#1145 · George Meredith
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Comedy in Narrative', which 1879 novel by George Meredith applies his famous critical theory of the 'Comic Spirit' to expose social hypocrisy and male vanity?
items.explanation: The Egoist: A Comedy in Narrative (1879) incorporates Meredith's theory from his 1877 lecture 'On the Idea of Comedy', using civilized humor to unmask human egoism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1146 · George Meredith
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Kegan Paul in 1879, which George Meredith novel was praised by Robert Louis Stevenson as a supreme achievement in comic characterization?
items.explanation: The Egoist established Meredith's critical reputation. Stevenson famously reread it five times, declaring that Willoughby was a mirror reflecting every man's selfish weaknesses.

items.title: Quiz Q#1147 · George Meredith
items.stem: In which 1885 novel by George Meredith does the brilliant and witty Irish heroine Diana Warwick, trapped in an unhappy marriage, face social scandal after leaking a government cabinet secret to a newspaper editor?
items.explanation: Diana Warwick is the heroine of Diana of the Crossways (1885). The novel is based on the real-life Caroline Norton, who was falsely accused of leaking the repeal of the Corn Laws.

items.title: Quiz Q#1148 · George Meredith
items.stem: Based loosely on the sensational real-life story of Victorian feminist reformer Caroline Norton, which 1885 novel was George Meredith's greatest commercial and popular success?
items.explanation: Diana of the Crossways (1885) was serialized in The Fortnightly Review before being published in three volumes. It became Meredith's first runaway commercial bestseller.

items.title: Quiz Q#1149 · Jules Verne
items.stem: Which pioneering 19th-century French author inaugurated the Extraordinary Voyages (Voyages Extraordinaires) series with works like Journey to the Center of the Earth (1864) and Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1870)?
items.explanation: Jules Verne (1828–1905) was the father of modern science fiction whose fifty-four Voyages Extraordinaires combined technological prophecy with thrilling geographic exploration.

items.title: Quiz Q#1150 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: In which series of provincial domestic chronicles by Margaret Oliphant—often compared to Anthony Trollope's Barsetshire novels—does Lucilla Marjoribanks scheme to become the social arbiter of local society?
options: Passages in the Life of Mrs. Margaret Maitland
items.explanation: The Chronicles of Carlingford (1861–1876) was Margaret Oliphant's celebrated series of six novels exploring ecclesiastical politics, family strife, and provincial life in the fictional town of Carlingford.

items.title: Quiz Q#1151 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Which prolific Scottish Victorian novelist created the Chronicles of Carlingford series and wrote over ninety novels, famously maintaining her family through unflagging contributions to Blackwood's Magazine?
items.explanation: Margaret Oliphant (1828–1897) was one of the most prolific Victorian women of letters, producing novels, biographies, and trenchant literary reviews for Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine.

items.title: Quiz Q#1152 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Serialized in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine between 1861 and 1876, which multi-volume fictional cycle by Margaret Oliphant includes Salem Chapel, The Rector, and Miss Marjoribanks?
items.explanation: Chronicles of Carlingford was serialized in Blackwood's, presenting a rich panoramic comedy of Anglican and Nonconformist religious society in provincial England.

items.title: Quiz Q#1153 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: In which 1866 novel by Margaret Oliphant does the calculating, confident heroine Lucilla Marjoribanks return from her Continental finishing school determined to 'be a comfort to dear papa' and manage the town's social life?
items.explanation: Miss Marjoribanks (1866) features Lucilla Marjoribanks, whose comic manipulation of Carlingford society is widely regarded as an ironic counterpart to Jane Austen's Emma.

items.title: Quiz Q#1154 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Often described by modern critics as a brilliant feminist parody of Victorian domestic duty, which 1866 novel by Margaret Oliphant features the indomitable Lucilla Marjoribanks?
items.explanation: Miss Marjoribanks was hailed by Q. D. Leavis as a masterpiece of Victorian comic irony, bridging the gap between Jane Austen's Emma and George Eliot's Dorothea Brooke.

items.title: Quiz Q#1155 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Serialized in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from February 1865 to May 1866, which novel is considered the crowning satirical triumph of Margaret Oliphant's Chronicles of Carlingford?
items.explanation: Miss Marjoribanks (1866) appeared in three volumes after running in Blackwood's, satirizing mid-Victorian domestic expectations through Lucilla's calculated social campaigns.

items.title: Quiz Q#1156 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: In which 1883 novel by Margaret Oliphant does the fiercely independent young heroine Hester Vernon reject charitable patronization from her wealthy banking cousin Catherine and seek meaningful paid employment?
items.explanation: Hester (1883) explores female economic independence and generational conflict between young Hester Vernon and the formidable matriarch Catherine Vernon, who manages the family bank.

items.title: Quiz Q#1157 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Which Victorian Scottish author wrote the 1883 novel Hester, exploring female autonomy, commercial speculation, and the rivalry between two strong-willed women in a provincial banking town?
items.explanation: Margaret Oliphant published Hester in 1883 with Macmillan, highlighting her recurring theme of energetic women constrained by limited Victorian social opportunities.

items.title: Quiz Q#1158 · Margaret Oliphant
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Macmillan in 1883, which later novel by Margaret Oliphant dramatizes the collapse of the Vernon family bank and the thwarted ambitions of its rebellious title heroine?
items.explanation: Hester (1883) subverted conventional Victorian romance endings: despite romantic proposals, the novel concludes with Hester remaining unmarried and self-reliant.

items.title: Quiz Q#1159 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: In Christina Rossetti's celebrated 1862 narrative poem Goblin Market, which sister succumbs to temptation by buying and eating the luscious fruit offered by the sinister goblin men?
items.explanation: Laura is the sister who trades a lock of her golden hair for the goblin fruit, falling wastefully ill until her sister Lizzie bravely redeems her by resisting the goblins.

items.title: Quiz Q#1160 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Illustrated with frontispiece designs by Dante Gabriel Rossetti and published in 1862, which groundbreaking fairy narrative by Christina Rossetti celebrates sisterly devotion and resistance to sensual temptation?
items.explanation: Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) established Christina Rossetti's fame. The title poem uses rapid, irregular dactylic rhythms to explore temptation, market commodification, and redemption.

items.title: Quiz Q#1161 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Which Victorian poet composed the famous sonnet 'Remember', opening with the poignant plea: "Remember me when I am gone away, / Gone far away into the silent land"?
items.explanation: Christina Rossetti wrote the Petrarchan sonnet 'Remember' in 1849 at age nineteen, publishing it in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862).

items.title: Quiz Q#1162 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Which 1862 poetry volume by Christina Rossetti was the first literary publication to bring widespread public recognition and commercial success to the Pre-Raphaelite aesthetic movement?
options: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems
items.explanation: Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) published by Macmillan was a major milestone, containing celebrated lyrics like 'Up-hill', 'Remember', 'A Birthday', and 'An Apple Gathering'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1163 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: In which 1866 allegorical narrative poem by Christina Rossetti does an indecisive prince dally along his journey with frivolous temptations, arriving only to find his royal bride has died waiting for him?
options: The Prince’s Progress and Other Poems
items.explanation: 'The Prince's Progress' (1866) was composed as a companion narrative to 'Goblin Market', dramatizing moral procrastination and spiritual failure.

items.title: Quiz Q#1164 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Which Victorian poet composed the haunting dirge in 'The Prince's Progress' that grieves for the bride: "Too late for love, too late for joy, / Too late, too late! / You loitered on the road too long..."?
items.explanation: This poignant dirge is sung by the bridal attendants in Christina Rossetti's 'The Prince's Progress' (1866) when the tardy prince finally reaches the palace.

items.title: Quiz Q#1165 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Published by Macmillan in 1866 with woodcut illustrations by her brother Dante Gabriel Rossetti, which was Christina Rossetti's second major poetry collection?
options: The Prince’s Progress and Other Poems
items.explanation: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems (1866) consolidated Christina Rossetti's reputation as a major Victorian devotional and lyric poet.

items.title: Quiz Q#1166 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: In which 1881 collection by Christina Rossetti does the fourteen-sonnet sequence 'Monna Innominata' give voice to the unnamed ladies celebrated by Dante and Petrarch, asserting female spiritual autonomy?
items.explanation: A Pageant and Other Poems (1881) contains 'Monna Innominata: A Sonnet of Sonnets', Rossetti's celebrated feminist response to courtly love poetry, giving voice to the silent muse.

items.title: Quiz Q#1167 · Christina Rossetti
items.stem: Which 1881 poetry collection by Christina Rossetti contains the sonnet of sonnets 'Monna Innominata' as well as the title masque poem of the twelve months?
items.explanation: A Pageant and Other Poems (1881) was Rossetti's last collection of secular and devotional verse, praised for its formal perfection in sonnet and ballata structures.

items.title: Quiz Q#1168 · Emily Dickinson
