items.stem: Which 19th-century American poet wrote the celebrated definition lyric opening with the lines: "'Hope' is the thing with feathers - / That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -"?
items.explanation: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) composed poem 254 ('Hope is the thing with feathers') around 1861, using common meter and her characteristic dashes.

items.title: Quiz Q#1169 · Emily Dickinson
items.stem: Published posthumously in Boston in 1890 by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, which volume first introduced the secluded Amherst poet's extraordinary verse to the reading public?
items.explanation: Poems (1890) was the first published gathering of Emily Dickinson's poetry, compiled four years after her death from the hand-sewn fascicles discovered in her bedroom.

items.title: Quiz Q#1170 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: In which 1865 children's classic by Lewis Carroll does a young girl fall down a rabbit-hole into a surreal underground world of talking animals, the Mad Hatter's tea party, and the Queen of Hearts?
items.explanation: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) by Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (Lewis Carroll) tells of Alice's dream journey through an anarchic world governed by linguistic riddles and nonsense.

items.title: Quiz Q#1171 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: Which Victorian author created the whimsical fantasy in which the young heroine, after growing to nine feet tall, famously exclaims: "Curiouser and curiouser!"?
items.explanation: Lewis Carroll coined the famous expression 'Curiouser and curiouser!' in Chapter 2 of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) as Alice consumes the cake marked 'EAT ME'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1172 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: Illustrated with forty-two iconic wood engravings by Sir John Tenniel and published in 1865, which masterpiece of Victorian nonsense literature was originated during a boat trip on the Thames for Alice Liddell?
items.explanation: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland was first told by Dodgson on 4 July 1862 during a rowing expedition with the Liddell sisters, before Macmillan published the Tenniel-illustrated book in 1865.

items.title: Quiz Q#1173 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: In which 1871 sequel by Lewis Carroll does Alice step through a drawing-room mirror into an alternative world structured as a giant game of chess, culminating in her becoming a Queen?
items.explanation: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There (1871) features chess-board geography, Tweedledum and Tweedledee, the White Knight, and the famous nonsense ballad 'Jabberwocky'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1174 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: Which Victorian author and Oxford logician composed the supreme nonsense poem 'Jabberwocky', opening with the line: "'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / Did gyre and gimble in the wabe"?
items.explanation: 'Jabberwocky' appears in Chapter 1 of Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871), celebrated as the greatest portmanteau nonsense poem in the English language.

items.title: Quiz Q#1175 · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Lewis Carroll / Charles Lutwidge Dodgson
items.stem: Published by Macmillan in December 1871 (dated 1872) with fifty illustrations by John Tenniel, which work contains the memorable poems 'Jabberwocky' and 'The Walrus and the Carpenter'?
items.explanation: Through the Looking-Glass was an instant commercial triumph in 1871, reuniting Carroll and illustrator Tenniel to bring Tweedledum, Humpty Dumpty, and the Red Queen to life.

items.title: Quiz Q#1176 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: In which classic 1868 American novel by Louisa May Alcott does the tomboyish, aspiring writer Jo March reject conventional marriage and devote herself to supporting her three sisters—Meg, Beth, and Amy?
items.explanation: Jo March is the fiercely independent protagonist of Little Women (1868–1869), modeled on Alcott herself, who sells her stories to help support her impoverished family during the Civil War.

items.title: Quiz Q#1177 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Which 19th-century American author opened her famous domestic novel with the complaining exclamation: "'Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents,' grumbled Jo, lying on the rug"?
items.explanation: This memorable opening line introduces the March sisters in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women (1868), establishing their family poverty and warm camaraderie.

items.title: Quiz Q#1178 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Published in two parts in 1868 and 1869 by Roberts Brothers of Boston, which classic bildungsroman by Louisa May Alcott follows the four March sisters growing up in Concord, Massachusetts?
items.explanation: Little Women (Part 1 in 1868, Part 2 as Good Wives in 1869) was an immediate literary sensation, selling thousands of copies and establishing Alcott's financial independence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1179 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: In which 1871 sequel by Louisa May Alcott do Jo March and her German husband, Professor Friedrich Bhaer, establish an unconventional, progressive boarding school for orphaned and unruly boys at Plumfield?
items.explanation: Little Men: Life at Plumfield with Jo's Boys (1871) depicts Jo and Professor Bhaer's loving educational experiment at Plumfield Estate, fostering character and practical skills.

items.title: Quiz Q#1180 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: In which novel by Louisa May Alcott does the orphaned street musician Nat Blake arrive seeking shelter with the timid query: "Please, sir, is this Plumfield?"?
items.explanation: Nat Blake's arrival opens Little Men (1871), setting the stage for Jo Bhaer's compassionate transformation of neglected boys into honorable young men.

items.title: Quiz Q#1181 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Subtitled 'Life at Plumfield with Jo's Boys', which 1871 novel by Louisa May Alcott drew on the progressive educational theories of her father, transcendentalist philosopher Bronson Alcott?
items.explanation: Little Men (1871) was written while Alcott was in Rome following the death of her sister May. It pays homage to Bronson Alcott's experimental Temple School educational methods.

items.title: Quiz Q#1182 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: In which 1886 novel concluding the March family saga do the grown-up Plumfield students—including Dan Kean, Nat Blake, and Tommy Bangs—face the challenges of college, careers, and romance?
items.explanation: Jo's Boys, and How They Turned Out (1886) concludes the trilogy, depicting Jo as a celebrated, weary author dealing with celebrity while guiding her grown students.

items.title: Quiz Q#1183 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Which American author concluded the March family trilogy in 1886 with Jo's Boys, wryly satirizing her own overwhelming real-life fame and the relentless demands of autograph seekers?
items.explanation: Louisa May Alcott inserted humorous semi-autobiographical scenes in Jo's Boys (1886), showing Jo Bhaer donning a disguise to avoid annoying literary tourists visiting Plumfield.

items.title: Quiz Q#1184 · Louisa May Alcott
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Louisa May Alcott
items.stem: Subtitled 'And How They Turned Out', which 1886 book was the third and final volume in Louisa May Alcott's beloved March family cycle?
items.explanation: Jo's Boys, and How They Turned Out (1886) was Alcott's final major novel, published two years before her death, chronicling the adulthood of the Plumfield alumni.

items.title: Quiz Q#1185 · William Morris
items.stem: In which monumental 1868–1870 verse collection by William Morris does the speaker introduce himself in the famous Apology as 'the idle singer of an empty day'?
items.explanation: The Earthly Paradise (1868–1870) is William Morris's epic storytelling collection framed on Chaucer's model, opening with the poet disclaiming power to heal modern social ills.

items.title: Quiz Q#1186 · William Morris
items.stem: Which Pre-Raphaelite poet, designer, and socialist pioneer opened his verse epic with the famous self-deprecating line: "Dreamer of dreams, born out of my due time, / Why should I strive to set the crooked straight? / Let it suffice me that my murmuring rhyme / Beats with light wing against the ivory gate, / The idle singer of an empty day"?
items.explanation: William Morris composed this celebrated Apology in The Earthly Paradise (1868–1870), contrasting medieval poetic romance with the harsh industrial realities of Victorian Britain.

items.title: Quiz Q#1187 · William Morris
items.stem: Structured like Chaucer's Canterbury Tales with twenty-four narrative tales alternating between classical Greek myths and medieval Norse/Germanic legends, which work was William Morris's greatest poetic success?
options: The Life and Death of Jason
items.explanation: The Earthly Paradise appeared in four volumes between 1868 and 1870, cementing Morris's contemporary reputation as one of the leading narrative poets of the Victorian era.

items.title: Quiz Q#1188 · William Morris
items.stem: In which 1890 utopian socialist romance by William Morris does the narrator William Guest fall asleep in Victorian London and awaken in the 21st century to find an idyllic, classless society living in harmony along the Thames?
options: The Story of the Glittering Plain
items.explanation: News from Nowhere: or, An Epoch of Rest (1890) depicts Morris's vision of an agrarian communist England where money, prisons, and industrial factories have been replaced by craftsmanship and communal fellowship.

items.title: Quiz Q#1189 · William Morris
items.stem: Serialized in the socialist journal Commonweal in 1890 as an explicit agrarian and aesthetic counterblast to Edward Bellamy's state-socialist novel Looking Backward, which utopian romance was written by William Morris?
options: The Well at the World's End
items.explanation: William Morris wrote News from Nowhere (1890) in Commonweal to counter Bellamy's mechanical, urbanized socialist utopia, presenting instead a decentralized, craft-based paradise.

items.title: Quiz Q#1190 · William Morris
items.stem: In which 1896 high fantasy prose romance by William Morris does Prince Ralph of Upmeads undertake an epic quest through medieval landscapes to drink from the magical waters that bestow long life and love?
options: The Well at the World’s End
The Story of the Glittering Plain
The Water of the Wondrous Isles
items.explanation: The Well at the World's End (1896) is one of Morris's pioneering fantasy romances, celebrated for establishing the conventions of secondary fantasy worlds that influenced J. R. R. Tolkien and C. S. Lewis.

items.title: Quiz Q#1191 · William Morris
items.stem: Printed at William Morris's famous Kelmscott Press in 1896 with woodcuts designed by Edward Burne-Jones, which high-fantasy romance is widely considered a foundational masterpiece of modern heroic fantasy?
options: The Story of the Glittering Plain
The Well at the World’s End
items.explanation: The Well at the World's End was published in a magnificent two-volume Kelmscott Press edition in 1896, showcasing Morris's archaic prose style and medieval typography.

items.title: Quiz Q#1192 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: In which 1876 novel by Mark Twain does an imaginative, mischievous boy in St. Petersburg, Missouri, whitewash Aunt Polly's fence, witness a graveyard murder, and hunt for Injun Joe's buried treasure?
items.explanation: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) introduces Tom Sawyer, Becky Thatcher, and Huckleberry Finn along the Mississippi River, celebrating boyhood adventure and frontier folklore.

items.title: Quiz Q#1193 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Which American humorist opened his classic boyhood adventure novel with Aunt Polly searching for the mischievous hero: "'Tom!' No answer. 'Tom!' No answer. 'What's gone with that boy, I wonder?'"?
items.explanation: Mark Twain opens The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) with Aunt Polly fruitlessly shouting for Tom, establishing the affectionate tension between adult authority and boyhood freedom.

items.title: Quiz Q#1194 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Published in 1876 by the American Publishing Company of Hartford, which classic picaresque tale by Mark Twain drew deeply upon the author's own childhood memories of Hannibal, Missouri?
items.explanation: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) transformed Twain's nostalgic reminiscences of Hannibal on the Mississippi into an enduring masterpiece of American literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1195 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: In which 1884 masterpiece by Mark Twain does the young narrator flee his abusive father and raft down the Mississippi River with the runaway enslaved man Jim, declaring: "All right, then, I'll go to hell"?
items.explanation: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) reaches its moral climax when Huck tears up his letter to Miss Watson, choosing to protect Jim from slavery even if it condemns his soul according to religious orthodoxy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1196 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Which American novelist created the iconic literary moment where the boy-narrator rejects society's racist moral code to protect his runaway friend Jim, proclaiming: "All right, then, I'll go to hell"?
items.explanation: Huck Finn's moral victory in Chapter 31 of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn represents what T. S. Eliot and Ernest Hemingway celebrated as the birth of modern American literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1197 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Hailed by Ernest Hemingway as the source of 'all modern American literature', which 1884 masterpiece by Mark Twain was first published in London by Chatto and Windus before its American release?
items.explanation: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was published in England in December 1884 and in the US in February 1885, pioneering vernacular first-person narrative in world literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1198 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: In which 1889 time-travel satire by Mark Twain is Hank Morgan, a practical Connecticut arms-factory superintendent, knocked unconscious and transported to 6th-century Camelot, where he uses modern science to rival the magician Merlin?
options: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court
items.explanation: Hank Morgan ('The Boss') is the protagonist of A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889), attempting to modernize feudal Britain with telegraphs, bicycles, and electricity before disaster strikes.

items.title: Quiz Q#1199 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Which 19th-century American satirist created the Connecticut factory foreman who introduces himself in Camelot: "I am an American... I was born and reared in Hartford, in the State of Connecticut... So I am a Yankee of the Yankees"?
items.explanation: Mark Twain puts this boast into the mouth of Hank Morgan in Chapter 1 of A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889), setting American pragmatism against chivalric feudalism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1200 · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mark Twain / Samuel Clemens
items.stem: Published in 1889 with satirical illustrations by Dan Beard, which novel by Mark Twain satirized Romantic medievalism, the divine right of kings, and Catholic church tyranny, ending in apocalyptic mechanized warfare?
options: Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc
A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court
items.explanation: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) began as a burlesque of Malory's Morte d'Arthur but darkened into a dystopian critique of industrial destruction at the Battle of the Sand-Belt.

items.title: Quiz Q#1201 · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.stem: In which sensational 1862 Victorian thriller does Lucy Graham—a fair, golden-haired governess married to the wealthy Sir Michael Audley—conceal her bigamous secret, set fire to an inn, and push her first husband into an old well?
items.explanation: Lucy Graham (Helen Talboys) is the scheming anti-heroine of Mary Elizabeth Braddon's sensation novel Lady Audley's Secret (1862). Her nephew-by-marriage Robert Audley unmasks her hidden crimes.

items.title: Quiz Q#1202 · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.stem: Which Victorian sensation novelist created the treacherous golden-haired bigamist Lady Audley, who confesses her desperate past and hereditary madness to Dr. Mosgrave?
items.explanation: Mary Elizabeth Braddon (1835–1915) established herself as the 'queen of sensation fiction' with Lady Audley's Secret (1862), subverting the Victorian ideal of the gentle domestic blonde angel.

items.title: Quiz Q#1203 · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.stem: Which 1862 three-volume blockbuster novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon became one of the greatest commercial sensations of the Victorian book trade, going through nine editions in its first three months?
items.explanation: Lady Audley's Secret was an enormous bestseller published by William Tinsley in 1862. It epitomized the sensation craze of the 1860s, combining domestic respectability with arson and murder.

items.title: Quiz Q#1204 · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.stem: In which 1863 sensation novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon does the high-spirited heiress Aurora Floyd find herself blackmailed by an uncouth groom whom she secretly married in her youth?
items.explanation: Aurora Floyd (1863) was Braddon's follow-up hit to Lady Audley's Secret. The equestrian heroine Aurora is blackmailed by the sinister groom James Conyers before his murder.

items.title: Quiz Q#1205 · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Mary Elizabeth Braddon
items.stem: Serialized in Temple Bar from January 1862 to January 1863, which second hit novel by Mary Elizabeth Braddon cemented her status alongside Wilkie Collins as a master of Victorian sensation fiction?
items.explanation: Aurora Floyd (1863) explored female passion, bigamy, and turf-racing culture, provoking debate among Victorian moralists while drawing thousands of eager readers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1206 · Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)
items.stem: In which 1872 satirical utopian novel by Samuel Butler does an unnamed traveler discover an upside-down civilization beyond the mountains where illness is treated as a criminal offense and crime as a medical disease?
items.explanation: Erewhon: or, Over the Range (1872) is Samuel Butler's anagrammatic satire ('nowhere' backwards). In Erewhon, sick citizens are jailed while embezzlers receive visits from moral 'straighteners'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1207 · Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)
items.stem: Published anonymously by Trübner & Co. in 1872, which Victorian satire contains the celebrated chapters on 'The Book of the Machines', predicting that conscious machines would eventually supersede humanity?
items.explanation: Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872) featured 'The Book of the Machines', an astonishingly prophetic philosophical critique of evolutionary mechanics and emerging artificial intelligence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1208 · Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)
items.stem: In which semi-autobiographical Victorian novel by Samuel Butler does the sensitive hero Ernest Pontifex struggle against the tyrannical religious hypocrisy of his clerical father, Theobald Pontifex?
items.explanation: Ernest Pontifex is the autobiographical protagonist of Samuel Butler's The Way of All Flesh (written 1873–1884, published 1903). The novel is a scathing satire of Victorian family hypocrisy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1209 · Samuel Butler (Victorian, 1835–1902)
items.stem: Written between 1873 and 1884 but suppressed until 1903 following the author's death, which novel by Samuel Butler attacked Victorian family tyranny and influenced George Bernard Shaw and modernism?
items.explanation: The Way of All Flesh (1903) was published posthumously by R. A. Streatfeild. Bernard Shaw hailed it as an iconoclastic masterpiece that shattered Victorian patriarchal illusions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1210 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: In which 1875 comic courtroom operetta by W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan does the jilted bride Angelina sue her fickle fiancé Edwin for breach of promise of marriage?
items.explanation: Trial by Jury (1875) was Gilbert and Sullivan's first major hit, a one-act dramatic cantata where the corrupt Learned Judge resolves the breach of promise suit by marrying the plaintiff himself.

items.title: Quiz Q#1211 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: In which satirical operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan does the unscrupulous Learned Judge confess his rise to legal prominence, singing: "And I fell in love with a rich attorney's / Elderly, ugly daughter"?
items.explanation: The Learned Judge's comic autobiographical song in Trial by Jury (1875) satirizes nepotism and self-interest in the Victorian legal system.

items.title: Quiz Q#1212 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: First performed at London's Royalty Theatre in March 1875 as an afterpiece to Offenbach's La Périchole, which operetta established the legendary partnership of W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan?
items.explanation: Trial by Jury (1875) was brought to the stage by impresario Richard D'Oyly Carte, launching the extraordinary collaboration that created the Savoy Operas.

items.title: Quiz Q#1213 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: In which 1878 nautical comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan does the pompous First Lord of the Admiralty, Sir Joseph Porter, admit that he became ruler of the Queen's Navee without ever going to sea?
items.explanation: Sir Joseph Porter, KCB, is the satirical target in H.M.S. Pinafore (1878), poking fun at W. H. Smith, a civilian bookseller appointed First Lord of the Admiralty by Disraeli.

items.title: Quiz Q#1214 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Which Gilbert and Sullivan patter song contains the satirical political advice: "Stick close to your desks and never go to sea, / And you all may be Rulers of the Queen's Navee!"?
items.explanation: This famous chorus concludes Sir Joseph Porter's song in H.M.S. Pinafore (1878), ridiculing political patronage and ministerial appointments based on party loyalty.

items.title: Quiz Q#1215 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Subtitled 'The Lass That Loved a Sailor', which 1878 comic opera premiered at the Opera Comique and ran for 571 performances, sparking an international Gilbert and Sullivan craze?
items.explanation: H.M.S. Pinafore (1878) transformed British light opera, combining Gilbert's topsy-turvy social satire of class barriers with Sullivan's infectious melodies.

items.title: Quiz Q#1216 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: In which 1879 comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan is the duty-bound hero Frederic mistakenly apprenticed until his twenty-first birthday to a band of soft-hearted maritime brigands?
items.explanation: The Pirates of Penzance (1879) turns on the comic predicament of Frederic, whose nursemaid mistakenly apprenticed him to a 'pirate' instead of a 'pilot', and whose leap-year birthday binds him to age 84.

items.title: Quiz Q#1217 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Which comic opera features the swashbuckling pirate leader singing: "Oh, better far to live and die / Under the brave black flag I fly, / Than play a sanctimonious part / With a pirate head and a pirate heart... For I am a Pirate King!"?
items.explanation: The Pirate King's anthem opens Act I of Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance (1879), satirizing Victorian moral hypocrisy in commerce and politics.

items.title: Quiz Q#1218 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Premiered at the Fifth Avenue Theatre in New York on 31 December 1879 to secure American copyright, which Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera features the iconic Major-General's Song?
items.explanation: The Pirates of Penzance: or, The Slave of Duty had its official premiere in New York in 1879 to preempt American copyright pirates, introducing Major-General Stanley's famous patter song.

items.title: Quiz Q#1219 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: In which 1885 Savoy Opera by Gilbert and Sullivan does the Emperor's son Nanki-Poo disguise himself as a wandering second trombonist to escape marriage with the elderly Katisha in the town of Titipu?
items.explanation: Nanki-Poo is the romantic lead in The Mikado (1885). Disguised as a minstrel, he seeks his beloved Yum-Yum, who is betrothed to Ko-Ko, the newly appointed Lord High Executioner.

items.title: Quiz Q#1220 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Which Gilbert and Sullivan opera opens in the fictional Japanese town of Titipu with the Japanese nobles proclaiming: "If you want to know who we are, / We are gentlemen of Japan; / On many a vase and jar, / On many a screen and fan"?
items.explanation: The Mikado (1885) opened at the Savoy Theatre, using a fantastical Japanese setting to parody British institutions, bureaucratic absurdities, and Victorian capital punishment.

items.title: Quiz Q#1221 · W. S. Gilbert
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · W. S. Gilbert
items.stem: Subtitled 'The Town of Titipu', which 1885 production was the most successful of all Gilbert and Sullivan operas, running for an unprecedented 672 performances at the Savoy Theatre?
items.explanation: The Mikado (1885) became a worldwide cultural phenomenon, celebrated for Ko-Ko's 'Little List' and 'Tit-willow' songs, and the Mikado's goal to 'make the punishment fit the crime'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1222 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: In which twelve-part poetic cycle by Alfred Tennyson does King Arthur attempt to establish a sacred, civilized realm at Camelot, only to witness its moral unraveling through the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere?
items.explanation: Idylls of the King (published in stages between 1859 and 1885) retells Arthurian legend in blank verse, presenting Arthur as the ideal soul warring with human passion and social decay.

items.title: Quiz Q#1223 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: Composed in blank verse over more than thirty years, which monumental Arthurian epic by Victorian Poet Laureate Alfred Tennyson was dedicated to Prince Albert after his death in 1861?
items.explanation: Tennyson dedicated Idylls of the King to the memory of Prince Albert ('These to His Memory—since he held them dear'), identifying Albert with Arthur as an exemplar of noble manhood.

items.title: Quiz Q#1224 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: In which profound 1850 elegy did Alfred Tennyson mourn the sudden death of his close Cambridge friend Arthur Henry Hallam, grappling with geological time, evolutionary doubt, and spiritual faith?
items.explanation: In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850) consists of 133 cantos written in the distinctive 'In Memoriam stanza' (ABBA iambic tetrameter), chronicling seventeen years of mourning from 1833 to 1849.

items.title: Quiz Q#1225 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: Published anonymously in May 1850 in the distinctive ABBA iambic tetrameter stanza, which masterpiece directly secured Alfred Tennyson's appointment as Queen Victoria's Poet Laureate?
items.explanation: In Memoriam was published by Edward Moxon in 1850. Queen Victoria found immense solace in its verses after Prince Albert's death, and Tennyson was named Poet Laureate that November.

items.title: Quiz Q#1226 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: In which celebrated 1842 dramatic monologue by Alfred Tennyson does an aged king of Ithaca reject passive domestic retirement to urge his mariners: "To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield"?
items.explanation: Tennyson composed 'Ulysses' in blank verse in October 1833 shortly after learning of Arthur Hallam's death, expressing the indomitable will to go forward in the face of loss.

items.title: Quiz Q#1227 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: Which Victorian Poet Laureate concluded his famous dramatic monologue of heroic endurance with the iconic line: "Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will / To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield"?
items.explanation: This famous closing line concludes Alfred Tennyson's 'Ulysses' (published in Poems, 1842), carved on the memorial cross for Captain Robert Falcon Scott in Antarctica.

items.title: Quiz Q#1228 · Alfred Tennyson
items.stem: Composed in the immediate aftermath of Arthur Hallam's death in October 1833 and published in Poems (1842), which Tennyson monologue drew on Dante's Inferno (Canto 26) rather than Homer's Odyssey?
items.explanation: Tennyson's 'Ulysses' was directly inspired by Dante's portrayal of Ulisse sailing past the Pillars of Hercules in search of forbidden knowledge, rather than Homer's home-loving hero.

items.title: Quiz Q#1229 · Anne Bronte
items.stem: In Anne Brontë's novel The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, under what assumed name does Helen Huntingdon live in secluded poverty at Wildfell Hall to hide from her dissipated husband?
items.explanation: Helen Huntingdon flees Grassdale Manor with her young son Arthur and takes up residence at the ruined Elizabethan mansion Wildfell Hall under the alias Helen Graham, earning a living as an artist.

items.title: Quiz Q#1230 · Anne Bronte
items.stem: Which 1848 novel by Anne Brontë was suppressed by her sister Charlotte Brontë after Anne's death on the grounds that 'the choice of subject was an entire mistake'?
items.explanation: After Anne's death in 1849, Charlotte Brontë withheld The Tenant of Wildfell Hall from republication, uncomfortable with its graphic depiction of Branwell Brontë's alcoholism and debauchery.

items.title: Quiz Q#1231 · Charlotte Bronte
items.stem: In which 1847 masterpiece by Charlotte Brontë does an orphaned, plain governess assert her moral equality at Thornfield Hall, declaring to Edward Rochester: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will"?
items.explanation: Jane Eyre is the fiercely principled heroine of Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847). Her moral autonomy leads her to leave Rochester when she discovers his mad wife, Bertha Mason, in the attic.

items.title: Quiz Q#1232 · Charlotte Bronte
items.stem: Published in October 1847 by Smith, Elder under the masculine pseudonym 'Currer Bell', which novel carried the famous subtitle 'An Autobiography'?
items.explanation: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography was an instant bestseller in 1847, celebrated for its revolutionary first-person female voice and passionate claim for female emotional equality.

items.title: Quiz Q#1233 · Charlotte Bronte
items.stem: In which 1853 psychological novel by Charlotte Brontë does the reserved, self-reliant Englishwoman Lucy Snowe teach English at Madame Beck's boarding school in the fictional Belgian city of Villette?
items.explanation: Lucy Snowe is the complex narrator of Villette (1853), drawing on Charlotte Brontë's own unrequited passion for Constantin Héger at the Pensionnat Héger in Brussels.

items.title: Quiz Q#1234 · Charlotte Bronte
items.stem: Ending with an ambiguous storm at sea that leaves the fate of Monsieur Paul Emanuel unresolved, which 1853 novel is regarded by George Eliot and modern critics as Charlotte Brontë's finest achievement?
items.explanation: Villette (1853) concluded with Charlotte Brontë's famous deliberate ambiguity regarding Paul Emanuel's survival, preserving Lucy Snowe's hard-won professional and economic autonomy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1235 · Emily Bronte
items.stem: In which 1847 masterpiece by Emily Brontë does the tenant Mr. Lockwood rent Thrushcross Grange and suffer terrifying nightmares of a ghost tapping at the window at the isolated farmhouse of Wuthering Heights?
items.explanation: Lockwood's visit in the opening chapters of Wuthering Heights (1847) introduces the multi-layered frame narrative, through which the housekeeper Nelly Dean recounts the fierce passion of Heathcliff and Catherine Earnshaw.

items.title: Quiz Q#1236 · Emily Bronte
items.stem: Published under the pen name 'Ellis Bell' in December 1847, which was Emily Brontë's sole novel, set on the wild Yorkshire moors and exploring the cosmic passion between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff?
items.explanation: Wuthering Heights (1847) is Emily Brontë's only novel, renowned for its complex chronological structure, elemental symbolism, and Catherine's declaration: 'I am Heathcliff!'

items.title: Quiz Q#1237 · Henry Lawson
items.stem: In which 1896 short story collection by Australian bush writer Henry Lawson does 'The Drover's Wife' stoically guard her children from a venomous black snake in an isolated bark humpy while her husband is away?
items.explanation: While the Billy Boils (1896) gathered Henry Lawson's pioneering bush realism, including 'The Drover's Wife' and 'The Union Buries Its Dead', foundational to Australian national literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1238 · Henry Lawson
items.stem: Which Australian short-story writer and poet captured the harsh isolation of the outback in While the Billy Boils, observing of the bush mother: "She is used to being left alone. She once lived nineteen months without seeing another human being"?
items.explanation: Henry Lawson (1867–1922) pioneered Australian bush realism in 'The Drover's Wife' (1892), depicting the lonely resilience of women in the outback.

items.title: Quiz Q#1239 · Henry Lawson
items.stem: Published in Sydney in 1896 by Angus and Robertson, which collection of fifty-two bush sketches and stories established Henry Lawson as the foremost voice of Australian democratic realism?
items.explanation: While the Billy Boils (1896) established Lawson's celebrated creed of 'mateship' and unromanticized frontier realism, marking a vital turning point in colonial Australian literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1240 · Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
items.stem: In which 1864 debut novel—the first Indian novel written in English—does the courageous heroine Matangini risk her life in the night to thwart her brutal husband Rajmohan's conspiracy against Madhav Ghose?
items.explanation: Rajmohan's Wife (1864) by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay is the historic first novel written in English by an Indian, centered on the defiant heroine Matangini.

items.title: Quiz Q#1241 · Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
items.stem: Serialized in the Calcutta weekly periodical Indian Field in 1864, which pioneering text by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay holds the historic distinction of being the first English novel by an Indian author?
items.explanation: Rajmohan's Wife was serialized in Kishori Chand Mitra's Indian Field in 1864 before Bankim turned to Bengali to write Durgeshnandini (1865), establishing modern Indian prose fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1242 · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.stem: In which 1865 historical romance by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay does the Mughal general's son, Rajput prince Jagat Singha, fall in love with Tilottama, the daughter of the fort commander Virendra Singha?
items.explanation: Durgeshnandini ('The Chieftain's Daughter', 1865) was Bankim's first Bengali novel, an influential historical romance set in 16th-century Bengal under Akbar's general Man Singh.

items.title: Quiz Q#1243 · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.stem: Meaning 'The Daughter of the Fort's Lord' and inspired by the historical romances of Sir Walter Scott (notably Ivanhoe), which 1865 work by Bankim Chandra inaugurated the modern novel in Indian vernacular literature?
items.explanation: Durgeshnandini (1865) created a sensation in Bengal. Bankim's dynamic Bengali prose style and romantic narrative structure earned him the title 'the Walter Scott of Bengal'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1244 · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.stem: In which 1882 patriotic novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay does the landlord Mahendra join Satyananda's band of sannyasi rebels dedicated to liberating the Motherland from famine and oppression?
items.explanation: Anandamath ('The Abbey of Bliss', 1882) is Bankim's famous political novel set during the Bengal Famine of 1770, depicting the Santan rebellion of sannyasis.

items.title: Quiz Q#1245 · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
items.stem: Which 1882 historical novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay incorporates the iconic national hymn 'Vande Mataram' ('Hail to thee, Mother'), transforming patriotic devotion into religious worship of the Motherland?
items.explanation: Anandamath (1882) introduced 'Vande Mataram', which became the supreme rallying anthem of the Indian independence movement and later India's official National Song.

items.title: Quiz Q#1246 · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.stem: In which dashing 1867 military romance by Ouida does the aristocratic guardsman Bertie Cecil take the blame for his brother's forgery, fleeing England to enlist under an assumed name in the French Foreign Legion in Algeria?
items.explanation: Bertie Cecil ('Beauty of the Brigades') is the chivalric hero of Ouida's Under Two Flags (1867), joined by Cigarette, the passionate French camp-follower who sacrifices her life for him.

items.title: Quiz Q#1247 · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.stem: Which flamboyant Victorian romantic novelist created the French Foreign Legion hero Bertie Cecil and his heroic comrade Cigarette in the 1867 classic Under Two Flags?
options: Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.explanation: Ouida (Marie Louise de la Ramée, 1839–1908) achieved international renown with Under Two Flags (1867), defining the glamorous, melodramatic genre of military romance.

items.title: Quiz Q#1248 · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in 1867, which military romance by Ouida is celebrated as the definitive Victorian novel of the French Foreign Legion and desert adventure?
items.explanation: Under Two Flags (1867) became one of the most widely adapted adventure novels of the 19th century, inspiring numerous stage melodramas and early Hollywood films.

items.title: Quiz Q#1249 · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.stem: In which 1880 society novel by Ouida is the pure and innocent young heroine Vere Herbert forced by her vain, selfish mother into an abusive marriage with the corrupt Russian prince Sergius Zouroff?
items.explanation: Vere Herbert is the noble heroine of Ouida's Moths (1880), enduring domestic cruelty from Prince Zouroff until rescued by her true love, the singer Lord Corrèze.

items.title: Quiz Q#1250 · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Ouida / Marie Louise de la Ramée
items.stem: Which 1880 high-society satire by Ouida launched a scathing attack on the corrupt morality, greed, and arranged marriages of the fashionable Anglo-European aristocracy?
items.explanation: Moths (1880) was one of Ouida's most passionate social critiques, portraying aristocratic European high society as frivolous moths fluttering destructively around the candle of vanity.
